البرهان قائد الجيش السوداني تم تحديثه الأربعاء 2026/10/21 07:27 م بتوقيت أبوظبي "الوجوه الغريبة" تعبير يستخدمه الجيش السوداني وكتائب الإخوان كذريعة لقتل مئات المدنيين في الأيام الأخيرة، وفق خبير. وتصاعدت الهجمات على الأسواق والمناطق المأهولة بالسكان في كردفان (جنوب) ودارفور (غرب)، والتي أسفرت عن سقوط مئات القتلى والجرحى. إدانة حقوقية وأدانت 3 منظمات حقوقية سودانية ودولية تصاعد الهجمات الجوية والمدفعية المكثفة التي قالت إن "الجيش السوداني يشنها بالتنسيق الميداني المباشر مع الكتائب والميليشيات العسكرية التابعة لتنظيم الإخوان، التي أسفرت عن سقوط مئات القتلى والجرحى في أوساط المدنيين بفضائح إنسانية متتالية في مناطق غرب كردفان وجنوب دارفور". وأفادت المنظمة السودانية لحقوق الإنسان "شرا"، ومنظمة "قادم" لتمكين اللاجئين، والمنظمة الأفريقية للحقوق والتنمية "أفورد"، في بيان مشترك، بأن "الغارات الجوية والهجمات بالطائرات المُسيّرة استهدفت بشكل مباشر تجمعات المدنيين والأسواق المكتظة". وأشارت إلى استهداف حافلة نقل تجارية تقل نساء وأطفالا وطلابا في محلية الدبب بغرب كردفان، ما أدى إلى سقوط أكثر من 300 قتيل وجريح، إلى جانب القصف الدموي على سوق مدينة المجلد وسوق المواشي في نيالا الذي خلف نحو 130 قتيلا وجريحا، إضافة إلى الاستهداف المتكرر لأسواق النهود وأبو زبد. وأضافت: "تعد كتائب الإخوان المسلمين المسلحة وفي مقدمتها ميليشيات البراء بن مالك وأذرع الحركة الإسلامية شريكا فعليا وميدانيا في التخطيط والتنفيذ لهذه الهجمات العشوائية التي تستهدف الأعيان المدنية والمناطق المأهولة بالسكان، عبر الاستمرار في تجييش الصراع وإجهاض مساعي التهدئة لحساب أجندات حزبية ضيقة". وطالبت المنظمات الحقوقية الأمم المتحدة ومجلس حقوق الإنسان والاتحاد الأفريقي بفتح تحقيقات دولية مستقلة وشفافة لملاحقة قيادات الجيش وحلفائهم، ومحاسبة كافة المتورطين في ارتكاب جرائم الحرب والانتهاكات الصارخة للقانون الدولي الإنساني. وجوه غريبة من جانبه، قال النجمي عثمان، المحلل السياسي السوداني، لـ"العين الإخبارية": "منذ أن أشعل جيش الحركة الإسلامية والإخوان الحرب في السودان في 15 أبريل/نيسان 2023، ظل الجيش يستهدف المواطنين بصورة مباشرة، وكان يصفهم بأنهم حواضن الدعم السريع، كما أطلق عليهم وصف الوجوه الغريبة". وأضاف: "كل شخص لا ينتمي إلى هذه الجماعة، أو لا يدعمها إعلاميا أو عسكريا، أو لا يستنفر لصالحها، يعد في نظرها من الوجوه الغريبة، ولا سيما الأشخاص القادمين من غرب السودان، وتحديدا دارفور وكردفان". وتابع: "ظل الجيش يرتكب هذه الانتهاكات، بدءًا من ولاية الجزيرة (وسط)، مرورا بالخرطوم، وتحديدا منطقة مايو وجنوب الحزام، وصولا إلى الحاج يوسف". وقال: "يقصف الطيران الحربي والطائرات المسيّرة المدنيين الأبرياء، فيما تتولى قوات على الأرض، بينها كتائب البراء وغيرها من الحركات التي وصفها بحركات الارتزاق، عمليات الذبح والتنكيل". وأوضح أن "آخر هذه الانتهاكات كان ما حدث في مدينة الدبيبات، وكذلك مدينة الضعين، وسوق المواشي في نيالا، وسوق النعام في جنوب كردفان". وقال: "خلال هذا الأسبوع، وصل رصد أعداد القتلى المدنيين إلى 1340 شخصا، من الأطفال والنساء وكبار السن والرجال وغيرهم، في الأسواق التي استُهدفت في كردفان وجنوب كردفان وشمال كردفان، بما في ذلك أبو زبد ونيالا والضعين". جرائم متواصلة وأكد أنه "في مدينة سودري بشمال كردفان، دخلت حركات الارتزاق، كان الطيران يضرب من الجو، فيما كانت تلك الحركات تذبح المواطنين على الأرض. دخل أفراد منها منازل المواطنين، وصوّروا أنفسهم داخلها، وتحدوا النساء المقيمات فيها، مطالبين إياهن بالعودة إلى منطقة سودري، ووجهوا إليهن تحديا مباشرا وتهديدا، قائلين لهن حرفيا: "تعالين إلى بيوتكن إن والجماعات الإرهابية. وشارك سالم، مترئسًا وفد السودان، في أعمال الاجتماع الـ21 لوزراء خارجية دول السوق المشتركة للشرق والجنوب الأفريقي “الكوميسا”، المنعقد في العاصمة الزيمبابوية هراري. ودعا محي الدين سالم، خلال حديثه في الاجتماع، إلى تشكيل “آلية إقليمية موحدة للتعامل مع التحديات الأمنية والسياسية، ومواجهة الحركات المتمردة والجماعات الإرهابية العابرة للحدود التي تستغل الأزمات لتهريب السلع والإضرار بالاستقرار الاقتصادي ورفع تكاليف المعيشة”. وطالب بضرورة تكامل جهود دول المنطقة لمكافحة الجريمة المنظمة والاتجار بالمخدرات، والتصدي للمخاطر التي تهدد المجتمعات الأفريقية، خاصة النساء والشباب وكبار السن، في ظل استغلال أوضاع الفقر والهشاشة. وأشار إلى أن استقرار دول المنطقة يمثل شرطًا أساسيًا لنجاح جهود التكامل الاقتصادي، وتعزيز التجارة البينية، وتحقيق الأمن الغذائي، وحماية الحدود. وحث دول الكوميسا على توحيد الرؤى والمواقف إزاء التهديدات المشتركة، بما يعزز قدرة القارة على معالجة أزماتها وتحقيق الاستقرار المستدام. وقال الوزير بحسب بيان لوزارة الخارجية إن موقف السودان ثابت حيال توصيف قوات الدعم السريع بأنها «مليشيا متمردة» في الأدبيات والمداولات الإقليمية، نظرًا إلى الجرائم والانتهاكات الجسيمة التي ارتكبتها بحق المدنيين، إضافة إلى ما وصفه بالدمار الممنهج للبنية التحتية. ودعا وزراء خارجية دول الكوميسا إلى زيارة العاصمة الخرطوم للوقوف ميدانيًا على حجم الدمار والآثار التي خلفتها اعتداءات قوات الدعم السريع على البلاد ومؤسساتها. ويخوض الجيش السوداني، منذ 15 أبريل 2023، حربًا ضد قوات الدعم السريع، اندلعت في الخرطوم، قبل أن تنحصر بصورة رئيسية في إقليمي كردفان والنيل الأزرق، فيما لا يزال معظم إقليم دارفور تحت سيطرة قوات الدعم السريع. وقالت وزارة الخارجية، في بيان، إن اجتماع الكوميسا أجاز التوصيات الواردة في تقرير حالة السلم والأمن في السودان والمنطقة. وأفادت بأن التوصيات شملت احترام سيادة السودان ووحدة أراضيه واستقلال مؤسساته الوطنية، علاوة على الرفض التام للتدخلات الخارجية والإمدادات العسكرية والمالية للأطراف المسلحة والمليشيات. ودعت التوصيات، بحسب البيان، إلى تنسيق جهود الكوميسا والاتحاد الأفريقي والمبادرات الأفريقية الداعمة للسلام، وتجنب تعارض المسارات التفاوضية. وأوضحت الوزارة أن التوصيات تضمنت دعم الترتيبات الفنية واللوجستية لإعادة افتتاح المقر الدائم لمحكمة العدل التابعة للكوميسا في الخرطوم، إلى جانب حشد المؤسسات التنموية والقطاع الخاص الأفريقي للمساهمة في جهود التعافي وإعادة الإعمار في السودان. الكلمات: إعادة الإعمار في السودان الكوميسا قوات الدعم السريع محي الدين سالم وزارة الخارجية السودانية مقالات ذات صلة الجيش المصري يطلق النار على سيارات مهربين فيه الأعضاء الدائمون في مجلس الأمن الدولي، إلى جانب مسؤولين رفيعي المستوى من دول الجوار السوداني، لا سيما إثيوبيا وتشاد، لضمان رؤية إقليمية شاملة للحل. تهدف المشاورات الجارية في قصر الأمم إلى توحيد الدولية إلى خطوات عملية على الأرض. وأشار هافيستو إلى أن قيمة هذا اللقاء تكمن في القدرة على ترجمة الشعور بضرورة التحرك العاجل إلى أفعال ملموسة تنهي معاناة الشعب السوداني. حذر المبعوث الأممي من استمرار المتحدة إلى السودان، على ضرورة أن يكون لدى شركاء السودان الدوليين والإقليميين "التزام راسخ بإنهاء الحرب، وتخفيف معاناة الشعب السوداني، ودعم حقه في مستقبل يسوده السلام والأمن والكرامة في ظل سودان موحد". جاء ذلك خلال الاجتماع التشاوري حول تعزيز تنسيق مبادرات وجهود السلام في السودان، الذي عقد اليوم الأربعاء في مقر الأمم المتحدة بجنيف، بمشاركة ممثلين رفيعي المستوى من 22 دولة، إلى جانب الأمم المتحدة، والاتحاد الأفريقي، والاتحاد الأوروبي، والهيئة الحكومية الدولية المعنية بالتنمية (إيغاد)، وجامعة الدول العربية. يعد هذا الاجتماع السادس من نوعه، ويشكل آلية تنسيقية هامة تجمع الأطراف الدولية والإقليمية المشاركة في جهود حل النزاع في السودان، ولا يضم في مداولاته الحكومة السودانية أو قوات الدعم السريع، رغم أنه يتم التشاور مع أطراف النزاع قبل انعقاده واطلاعهم على نتائجه بعد اختتامه. وقد عقدت الاجتماعات السابقة في القاهرة، وجيبوتي، ونواكشوط، وبروكسل. وفي كلمته الافتتاحية، أكد هافيستو أن أصوات الشعب السوداني يجب أن توجه المداولات، وأن "تطلعاتهم يجب أن تظل المعيار الذي نقيس به مدى تقدمنا". وأوضح أن المناقشات ستتمحور حول جهود خفض التصعيد وبناء الثقة بين الأطراف، ومسار الانتقال نحو مرحلة سياسية انتقالية وعملية سياسية يقودها السودانيون، بالإضافة إلى الأبعاد الإقليمية للنزاع وكيفية منع تدهور الأوضاع وامتداد النزاع بشكل أكبر إلى الدول المجاورة. وأشار هافيستو إلى أن قيمة هذا الاجتماع تعتمد على قدرة المشاركين على تحويل الإدراك المشترك لمدى ضرورة التحرك العاجل إلى إجراءات عملية، قائلا: "نحن مدينون للشعب السوداني باهتمام مستمر، وانخراط متسق، وعمل حازم. ومع اقتراب شهر نيسان/أبريل 2027، يجب علينا بذل كل ما في وسعنا لضمان أن يشكل هذا التاريخ نقطة تحول نحو السلام، بدلا من أن يكون بداية لعام آخر من الحرب والمعاناة. إن هدفنا من هذا الاجتماع هو تسخير جهودنا الجماعية لخدمة الشعب السوداني". لا أحد بمنأى عن التبعات من جانبه، قال ألكسندر فاسيل، وزير الدولة السويسري للشؤون الخارجية، إنه بعد مرور 1285 يوما على الحرب في السودان، أصبحت اليوم "بالغة التعقيد وأكثر فتكا بكثير"، حيث تشهد البلاد واحدة من أسوأ الأزمات الإنسانية وأزمات الحماية في العالم. وأكد فاسيل أن سويسرا، التي شاركت في استضافة الاجتماع، ترى أن عملية السلام في السودان لن تنجح إلا إذا تضافرت المسارات الأمنية والسياسية والإنسانية. وفي حين يمثل السودان أكبر استجابة إنسانية لسويسرا في أفريقيا، فإن بلاده تواصل دورها كـ "جسر للتواصل وميسر للحوار"، حيث تجمع أطرافا سودانية في إطار غير رسمي للمساعدة في تهيئة الأرضية للمفاوضات السياسية الرسمية، بحسب الوزير السويسري. إلا أن فاسيل شدد على أن حماية المدنيين وتوفير الوصول الإنساني لا ينبغي أن ينتظرا التوصل إلى وقف إطلاق نار أو حل سياسي، وأضاف: "يعاني المدنيون وهم يفقدون حياتهم اليوم. لذا يجب على أطراف النزاع حمايتهم في جميع الأوقات وتحت أي ظرف، وتسهيل وصولهم إلى المساعدات الإنسانية". وفيما أقر بأن المشاركين في الاجتماع قد لا يتبنون وجهات نظر متطابقة حول ديناميكيات الوضع في السودان، إلا أنه رأى أن هناك اتفاقا عاما على عدم وجود حل عسكري للنزاع، وأن السبيل الوحيد لإنهائه بشكل دائم يكمن في دعم حوار شامل يقوده السودانيون أنفسهم. وقال في هذا الصدد: "لن يكون أي وفد في هذه القاعة بمنأى عن تبعات سودان ممزق يعاني من عنف ممتد كالذي نشهده حاليا. لذا، أدعو الجميع هنا إلى التحلي بالشجاعة والاتفاق على تكثيف جهودنا الجماعية". ♦ تحميل تطبيق أخبار الأمم المتحدة بالعربية من متجر آبل لأجهزة الأيفون والآيباد IOS أو من متجر غوغل لأجهزة أندرويد Android . ♦ الاشتراك في Attending Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations as President William Ruto’s guest of honour, Abiy emphasized the longstanding partnership between the two countries, highlighting cooperation in electricity, telecommunications, trade and regional connectivity. Yet beyond the diplomatic celebrations, the visit coincided with growing tensions involving Somalia, whose internal political crisis has begun complicating its relations with both Ethiopia and Kenya. Although Abiy’s visit was officially centered on Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations and bilateral cooperation, it unfolded against a backdrop of growing regional tensions involving Somalia. The visit did not publicly establish a common Ethiopian and Kenyan position on the Somali crisis, but it brought renewed attention to the strategic importance of their partnership as both countries navigate increasingly complicated relations with Mogadishu. The significance of Ethiopia’s relationship with Kenya extends beyond bilateral cooperation. Both countries have invested considerable military and diplomatic resources in Somalia’s stabilization, particularly in efforts to contain Al Shabaab and prevent insecurity from spreading across their borders. However, Somalia’s confrontation between its federal government and regional political actors is creating disagreements over the responsibilities of neighbouring countries. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to maintain its commitment to Somalia’s security without becoming involved in political disputes that could undermine its wider regional interests. The immediate source of tension lies in Somalia’s South West State, where the removal of former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March 2026 failed to produce a lasting political settlement. Instead, confrontations between his supporters and forces aligned with the federal government have continued, exposing deeper disagreements over regional autonomy and the distribution of political authority. By October 19, forces loyal to Laftagareen reportedly controlled five towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere and Dinsoor, complicating Mogadishu’s efforts to consolidate authority. The conflict is particularly consequential because the South West State includes territories where Ethiopian forces have maintained a security presence for years. According to Somali Guardian reporting published on October 19 , Somali federal authorities requested Ethiopian military assistance against forces aligned with Laftagareen, but Ethiopian commanders declined to participate in what they considered an internal political confrontation. Although the reported exchange has not been independently confirmed, it illustrates a fundamental question concerning foreign military involvement in Somalia: whether security assistance intended to confront common threats should extend to supporting the federal government in disputes over domestic political authority. For Ethiopia, the issue has acquired additional importance following the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, ATMIS, to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, which commenced on January 1, 2025. Under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2767 , the successor mission was authorized to support Somali forces against Al Shabaab, protect civilians and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali institutions. Its mandate also encompasses security support for political processes, but does not provide unrestricted authority to determine the outcome of internal political disputes. The transition brought renewed attention to the distinction between Ethiopian troops operating under African Union arrangements and those deployed through separate bilateral security understandings. This distinction matters because forces assigned to AUSSOM operate within a defined multinational framework, while deployments outside that structure depend on separate arrangements with Somalia. In its December 2025 communiqué , the African Union Peace and Security Council explicitly acknowledged Ethiopia and Uganda for deploying additional troops under bilateral arrangements. Their presence cannot therefore be understood solely through AUSSOM’s command structure. Ethiopia’s longstanding involvement in Somalia has primarily been driven by the need to prevent Al Shabaab from developing secure operating areas near Ethiopian territory. The group’s ability to exploit instability and threaten communities across borders makes developments in Somalia directly relevant to Ethiopia’s national security. Ethiopian military operations and participation in successive African Union missions have consequently contributed to a broader effort to contain threats before they reach Ethiopian territory. The South West State remains especially important because the Bay and Bakool regions form part of the wider security environment connected to Ethiopia’s eastern frontier. Participation in Somalia’s internal political confrontations, however, would expose Ethiopia to different risks. Military intervention could associate Ethiopian forces with one Somali political faction, weaken relationships with local communities and transform a defined security commitment into an extended responsibility for political outcomes. Even a successful intervention would not necessarily resolve disagreements concerning federal authority and regional political representation. Somalia’s domestic disputes require political settlements that military involvement by neighbouring countries cannot independently deliver. This position should not be confused with opposition to Somalia’s federal government. Addis Ababa and Mogadishu continue to maintain diplomatic relations and share an interest in preventing renewed militant expansion. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s September 29 visit to Addis Ababa , during which he discussed bilateral relations and regional security with Abiy Ahmed, demonstrated the continued importance of diplomatic engagement despite existing disagreements. Those disagreements nevertheless have a deeper history. The January 2024 memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland, which addressed potential Ethiopian maritime access, produced a significant confrontation with Mogadishu over sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somalia regarded the arrangement as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Ethiopia viewed access to the sea as an important strategic and economic objective. The dispute contributed to Somalia’s closer security engagement with Egypt, which already maintained long winded Nile disagreements with Ethiopia. The December 2024 Ankara Declaration , facilitated by Türkiye, helped restore diplomatic engagement by reaffirming mutual respect for sovereignty and acknowledging the possibility of mutually beneficial maritime arrangements under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Nevertheless, restoring diplomatic communication did not eliminate competing regional security calculations. Egypt’s expanding security engagement with Somalia and its prospective contribution to AUSSOM have introduced further sensitivity into discussions about troop deployments. The African Union’s June 2025 negotiations with troop-contributing countries included Ethiopia and Egypt, demonstrating that both countries were considered within the mission’s institutional arrangements. In December 2025, the African Union also acknowledged Egypt’s preparations for deployment while emphasizing the need to prevent security gaps during the transition. Political endorsement, negotiated contributions and actual troop deployments, however, remain distinct stages. For Ethiopia, any substantial expansion of Egyptian forces near areas where Ethiopian troops operate would raise operational questions, particularly given the unresolved Nile dispute. Careful coordination would be essential to prevent competing strategic interests from complicating counterterrorism operations. Kenya faces a related challenge arising from Somalia’s domestic political confrontation. Laftagareen’s presence in Kenya following his removal has generated criticism from Somali officials. On October 19, Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdikadir Mohamed Nur Jama, reportedly accused individuals residing in Kenya of involvement in activities connected to the conflict and questioned the alleged protection they received. The reporting did not establish evidence supporting those allegations, and Kenyan authorities had not publicly responded at the time. Hosting Somali political figures does not independently demonstrate Kenyan government support for their military activities. Nairobi must balance its diplomatic responsibilities and continued cooperation with Mogadishu against its own legal and national security considerations. The consequences of Somali instability for Kenya are also economic. The Lamu Port South Sudan Ethiopia Transport corridor, LAPSSET, represents an important regional infrastructure initiative intended to expand commercial connectivity and diversify access to maritime trade. Its security is connected to conditions in northern and coastal Kenya, where Al Shabaab has demonstrated the ability to threaten personnel and transport infrastructure. On September 19, 2026, suspected militants attacked Kenyan military personnel patrolling part of the corridor in Garissa. No casualties were reported, but the incident illustrated the security demands associated with protecting strategic infrastructure. Although these attacks cannot be directly attributed to the South West State’s political crisis, prolonged instability in Somalia could place additional pressure on counterterrorism operations and create opportunities for militant expansion. For Kenya, preserving security cooperation with Somalia therefore carries implications for domestic security, investment and regional transport connectivity. Ethiopia shares an interest in protecting these connections, which could strengthen economic integration and provide additional commercial routes. Against this background, the partnership between Addis Ababa and Nairobi offers continuity. Cooperation in electricity transmission, telecommunications and transport has created practical interests that extend beyond individual political disagreements. During his October 20 visit , Abiy emphasized Ethiopia’s electricity exports to Kenya, Safaricom’s presence in Ethiopia and growing commercial connections. Their importance becomes greater as Ethiopia confronts renewed tensions with Eritrea, instability in northern Ethiopia and unresolved strategic disagreements with Egypt. The October 2026 escalation in Tigray and tensions with Eritrea demonstrate the competing pressures confronting Addis Ababa. Strong relations with Kenya provide an additional channel for diplomatic consultation without requiring both governments to adopt identical policies toward Somalia. The coming months will test whether the three countries can prevent Somalia’s internal confrontation from developing into a wider regional dispute. Particular attention should be given to the security situation around Baidoa, changes to Ethiopian and Egyptian troop arrangements, and Somalia’s political preparations ahead of the presidential election announced for May 15, 2027 . Diplomatic engagement through Kenya, IGAD or other regional mechanisms could become increasingly relevant if political divisions deepen. Whether mediation initiatives emerge, however, will depend on the willingness of the parties to pursue negotiation. Abiy’s Kenya visit ultimately illustrates the continuing value of dependable regional partnerships during a period of uncertainty. Ethiopia’s national interests require a stable Somalia, effective cooperation against Al Shabaab and security arrangements that do not unnecessarily entangle Ethiopian forces in domestic political rivalries. Its relationship with Kenya offers opportunities to advance those objectives while protecting economic integration and regional connectivity. The challenge for Addis Ababa is to preserve this partnership alongside constructive engagement with Mogadishu, ensuring that Somalia’s political disagreements do not become another source of confrontation across the Horn of Africa. Convened in late 1996 under IGAD’s newly established conflict-resolution mandate, the talks culminated on 3 January 1997 in the creation of a 41-member National Salvation Council, with representation allocated to the four major clan families and smaller communities. Although Sodere did not produce a lasting government, it established a broad-based framework for political representation that subsequent reconciliation efforts would revisit The collapse of the Somali state in January 1991 left political authority dispersed among armed factions, while successive international efforts failed to establish a national government capable of consolidating control. The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1993 brought leading factions into a common framework, but agreement on paper did not resolve the struggle for power in Mogadishu; by the time the last United Nations troops withdrew in March 1995, the underlying competition remained intact. Rivalry between Ali Mahdi Mohamed and the Aideed camp, which passed to Hussein Aideed following General Mohamed Farah Aideed’s death in August 1996, continued to obstruct the emergence of a national political authority. The consequences extended beyond the capital. In the border region of Gedo, Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI) established a presence centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometers from Ethiopia, which Addis Ababa regarded as a base for a movement responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linked to other armed groups opposed to its government. Somalia’s fragmentation thus presented Ethiopia with a problem that international mediation alone had not resolved, the absence of a functioning state was not merely prolonging conflict within Somalia but also leaving neighboring territory exposed to armed networks that could operate across the border. This gave Ethiopia a direct security interest in the restoration of Somali political authority. The expansion of regional institutions in 1996 provided an important foundation for a more coordinated response to Somalia’s political fragmentation, creating a framework through which Ethiopia could address its security concerns while contributing to a regional effort to restore Somali political dialogue. Founded in 1986 as the Intergovernmental Authority on Drought and Development, with a mandate centred on drought and desertification, the organization was reconstituted as the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) following the amendment of its founding instrument in Nairobi on 21 March 1996 and its relaunch at the Djibouti summit of 25–26 November. The revised charter incorporated the prevention, management and resolution of inter-state and intra-state conflicts through dialogue, placing peace and security alongside food security and economic cooperation among the organization’s priorities. This change reflected a broader recognition that the conflicts confronting the Horn of Africa required regional mechanisms capable of addressing their political and security dimensions. For Ethiopia, whose border security was directly affected by the absence of effective authority in Somalia, IGAD’s expanded mandate offered a legitimate avenue for supporting reconciliation through regional diplomacy. The framework connected Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns with the wider regional interest in reducing conflict and restoring political order in Somalia, giving its diplomatic engagement an institutional foundation and a shared regional purpose. Although divisions among IGAD members, including the severance of relations with Sudan by Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda during the preceding year, complicated regional cooperation, the organization’s expanded mandate established an important basis for renewed engagement. OAU strengthened this framework in July 1996, when its Yaoundé resolution recognized Meles Zenawi, then outgoing OAU chairman, as holding a special mandate to facilitate peace in Somalia and supported efforts by IGAD member states to reactivate their initiatives. This endorsement connected the emerging regional effort to the OAU’s broader diplomatic role and reinforced the legitimacy of renewed attempts to bring Somali factions into negotiations. Ethiopia subsequently informed the United Nations Security Council that it had convened the Sodere conference in November 1996 in accordance with an IGAD mandate. Operating within this reinforced regional framework, Ethiopian conduct in the second half of 1996 ran along two tracks that differed in instrument yet converged through local partnerships. On the military track, Ethiopia acted against Al-Itihaad al-Islamiya (AIAI), an Islamist group that had established a presence in the Gedo region centered on Luuq, roughly ninety kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Addis Ababa regarded AIAI as a direct security threat, holding it responsible for attacks inside Ethiopia and linking it to other armed networks opposed to the Ethiopian government. Ethiopian forces therefore crossed into Gedo on 9 August 1996 to attack AIAI bases, and fighting continued through December. The fourth major assault on the group, launched on 11 June 1997, captured Luuq and Buulo Haawo and deprived AIAI of its last major bases in the region. This military campaign ran in parallel with a political initiative that sought to harness Somali opposition to AIAI and embed Ethiopia’s border-security objectives within a broader reconciliation process. On the political track, Ethiopia convened Somali leaders at the Sodere resort for roughly six weeks of talks, which ended on 3 January 1997 with a declaration signed by 27 leaders representing 26 factions. The declaration created a National Salvation Council of 41 members and a National Executive Committee of 11 members led by five co-chairmen, with authority to speak for the Council and to prepare a Transitional Central Authority or Provisional Central Government, and it committed the signatories to a National Reconciliation Conference at Bossaso. The Somali National Front, a competitor of AIAI for control of Gedo, was among the signatories. That overlap offered Somali opponents of AIAI an institutional route to national standing and tied a border security objective to a political process that Somali actors could own. The composition of the Council contains the process’s most durable contribution. Nine seats went to each of the four major clan families, Darod, Hawiye, Rahanweyn and Dir, and five to smaller groups, a distribution that totals 41 and approximates the half-share later formalized for minorities under the 4.5 formula. For the first time the Darod accepted parity among the main clan families. That principle of clan-family parity, first given institutional expression at Sodere, was subsequently formalized at the Arta conference in 2000 and then applied at scale by the Mbagathi process, which in 2004 allocated 61 seats to each of the four major families and 31 to the minority bloc within a 275-member Transitional Federal Parliament. By converting a contest over who speaks for Somalia into a bounded negotiation over who sits within each family’s allotment, parity supplied the mechanism through which Sodere moved Somali politics from open military competition toward transitional institutions. Sodere’s significance extended beyond the representational framework it helped establish to the regional diplomacy through which that framework was pursued. Ethiopia’s subsequent involvement in Somali reconciliation formed part of a recurring pattern that included hosting the 1993 Addis Ababa conference, convening Sodere in 1996 and 1997, participating in the IGAD-mediated Mbagathi talks that produced the Transitional Federal Charter in 2004, and contributing troops to the African Union missions in Somalia, AMISOM and ATMIS, and now AUSSOM. The Mbagathi record offers particularly clear evidence that Somali actors themselves regarded Ethiopia’s participation as consequential. In February 2004, six faction leaders of the Somali Restoration and Reconstruction Council announced that they would stay out of the final phase of the talks while Ethiopia was absent from the table. Hussein Aideed, who had succeeded his father General Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1996 and had remained outside the Sodere process the following year, now argued that a regional peace process required consensus among neighbouring states as well as among Somalis. His position marked a shift from contesting Ethiopia’s involvement in 1997 to treating the participation of neighboring states as a condition of a credible settlement, illustrating how the regional approach embodied at Sodere became an established feature of subsequent Somali peace negotiations. This historical experience has direct relevance as Somalia confronts a demanding security transition, with Al-Shabaab continuing to threaten state consolidation, domestic political negotiations remaining unsettled after the inconclusive May 2026 talks, and AUSSOM’s operational future facing growing financial uncertainty following Washington’s announced intention to end its support for UN logistics and operations from 2027. Ethiopia’s renewed commitment to AUSSOM, reaffirmed at the August 2026 troop-contributing countries summit, provides an important basis for strengthening this regional security relationship. Somalia’s current security transition increases the strategic importance of sustained coordination with Ethiopia. Al-Shabaab retains a presence in areas of Gedo and Bakool near the Ethiopian frontier, while Washington’s decision to end funding for UN logistical support to AUSSOM after December 2026 adds pressure to the mission’s operational continuity. These developments connect Somalia’s internal security challenges directly to the management of its western border, where gaps in territorial control can enable armed groups to move, reorganize and exploit weaknesses in coordination between security forces. Ethiopia’s direct exposure to these threats, its existing security involvement in Somalia and its capacity to operate along the shared frontier make bilateral cooperation consequential to how these risks are managed. For Mogadishu, the practical priority is to establish predictable arrangements with Addis Ababa for intelligence exchange, border threat assessment, troop coordination and consultation over operations affecting Somali territory. These mechanisms would help align Ethiopian security activities with federal priorities, improve continuity between bilateral cooperation and AUSSOM, and give Somali authorities greater influence over the regional response to threats within their jurisdiction. As Somalia assumes greater responsibility for its own security amid uncertainty over international support, the quality of its coordination with Ethiopia will directly affect its capacity to manage cross-border threats and sustain security across its western regions. A strategy designed to pressure the Ethiopian federal government by disrupting this vital trade route would have imposed costs on both countries, potentially extending Ethiopia’s conflict into a wider regional economic crisis. The corridor is not simply a transport link between two neighbouring states. It underpins Ethiopia’s access to international markets and Djibouti’s role as a principal gateway for Ethiopian trade. More than 95 per cent of Ethiopia’s import-export trade uses the Ethio-Djibouti corridor, while Djibouti’s economy relies heavily on Ethiopian trade through its port. A disruption would have threatened Ethiopia’s access to international markets while putting Djibouti’s port-related economic activity at risk. The scale of the impact would depend on the duration and extent of the disruption, but the corridor’s importance makes its security a shared economic concern. The plan must also be understood in the context of the military imbalance between the ENDF and the opposing forces. Given the ENDF’s apparent military superiority in conventional capabilities, direct confrontation with the Ethiopian military would have presented a significant challenge. Threatening the Ethio-Djibouti corridor could have offered the opposing forces an asymmetric means of exerting pressure on the federal government. This reflects a broader strategic logic: actors facing disadvantages in direct military confrontation may seek leverage by threatening infrastructure essential to a state’s economic functioning. The corridor represented precisely such a vulnerability. However, this strategic logic alone does not establish that a coordinated plan existed; that allegation must be assessed against the reported intelligence and subsequent battlefield developments. The corridor’s strategic significance also creates a constraint for any actor seeking to exploit it. Although disruption could impose economic costs on Ethiopia, it could simultaneously undermine Djibouti’s port revenues and commercial activity, potentially broadening opposition to the threat beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Such an outcome would risk turning an attempt to pressure the Ethiopian federal government into a wider regional security concern. The interdependence of the two economies therefore has a strategic dimension: the corridor’s vulnerability is not exclusively Ethiopia’s weakness, but also a source of shared interest in preventing its disruption. This makes the protection of the route relevant to regional stability as well as bilateral economic security. The leaked intelligence report suggests that Eritrean troops were present at 50 locations in Ethiopian territory across eastern Tigray and northern Afar before the Ethiopian government launched its defensive operation. According to the report, the deployment was intended to facilitate an attempt to cut the Ethio-Djibouti trade corridor. Subsequent reporting documented the TPLF-led forces’ advance into Afar, including the capture of Erebti and their movement towards Afdeera, underscoring the region’s strategic importance to Ethiopia’s access to Djibouti. These developments provide relevant context for assessing the alleged plan, although the reported troop deployments and rebel advances do not, on their own, establish that all the actors involved were coordinating towards that objective. The presence of Eritrean troops at these locations did not, in itself, guarantee control of the corridor. On 1 October 2026, federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force units counterattacked and retook both towns, reversing much of the rebel advance in Afar. The ENDF’s technological capabilities, intelligence-gathering capacity and operational reach may have contributed to its response, although the extent of their influence cannot be established from the reported battlefield outcome alone. Further evidence concerning force coordination, operational decisions and battlefield performance would be needed to determine the precise factors behind the reversal. The counteroffensive addressed the immediate battlefield situation, but it did not eliminate the broader security concern raised by the alleged plan. The intelligence report therefore raises questions about foreign military deployments near strategically sensitive areas and the potential threats they could pose to Ethiopia’s economic security. The episode underscored the importance of integrating critical transport infrastructure into national defence planning, intelligence collection and inter-agency coordination. Protecting the Ethio-Djibouti corridor requires identifying vulnerabilities before armed actors can exploit them, as well as maintaining the capacity to respond effectively to emerging threats. Its geographic exposure and economic importance make early warning and infrastructure resilience essential components of corridor security. Djibouti’s position is central to this assessment. Ethiopia should therefore approach corridor protection as a shared bilateral concern rather than solely as a domestic security matter. Structured cooperation could help both countries exchange relevant threat assessments, coordinate security planning and safeguard the trade relationship on which their mutual economic interests depend. At the national level, Ethiopia should make corridor security a permanent national-security priority through complementary measures. Coordinated military and intelligence planning should strengthen strategic warning and enable authorities to assess credible indications of armed movements towards corridor-adjacent areas, suspicious troop deployments and attempts to disrupt transport networks. Layered protection should improve the resilience of critical transport and logistics infrastructure, reducing the risk that disruption at a single point could interrupt the wider trade route. Periodic reviews of security conditions and corridor vulnerabilities would help ensure that these measures remain responsive to changing threats. The security of the Ethiopia-Djibouti trade corridor is inseparable from the strategic interests of both countries. Although the ENDF’s reported counteroffensive reversed rebel gains in Afar, the alleged plan and the reported Eritrean troop deployments warrant further scrutiny. Preventing future threats requires sustained defence preparedness, effective early warning and institutionalised bilateral security cooperation. Ultimately, safeguarding the corridor is essential to Ethiopia’s economic security, Djibouti’s commercial interests and regional stability. In a region plagued by persistent conflict, militant activities, and extremist and terrorist havens, the last thing it needs is another war. As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated , “the last thing the world needs right now is another war.” However, Ethiopia’s relationship with Eritrea does not seem likely to be resolved through conventional diplomatic assurances alone. Since its secession, Eritrea has adopted an antagonistic posture toward its largest neighbor and pursued policies that challenge Ethiopia’s security and regional interests. It has a documented record of supporting anti-Ethiopian government armed groups, providing them with sanctuary and other forms of assistance. Following the Pretoria peace agreement, although Eritrean forces withdrew from Tigray’s heartland, they remained in territories inside Tigray near the Eritrean border. Eritrea also established an alliance with the TPLF and other armed groups inside Ethiopian territory, with the latter forming an alliance aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian federal government. In this context, Eritrea plays a significant role, while other external actors also contribute by providing support. The nature of the Eritrean state under the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ) remains a persistent source of insecurity for Ethiopia. The country’s political system is highly centralized and militarized, with indefinite national service, the dominance of military institutions over civilian administration, and the concentration of power in President Isaias Afwerki and his close circle all playing a central role in keeping the regime in power. Since the 1998–2000 border war, Eritrea has maintained a security posture shaped by permanent mobilization and a deep suspicion of Ethiopia. This reflects what can be described as a small-state syndrome, in which the perceived vulnerability of a state, its limited strategic depth, and its exposure to stronger neighbors shape how its leadership understands external threats. In Eritrea’s case, this outlook has reinforced the tendency to view Ethiopia through a security lens and to treat the preservation of regime security as a national priority. This reinforces the need to address the underlying strategic calculations that shape Eritrea’s behavior toward Ethiopia. In recent years, the practical consequences of this structure have become evident in Eritrea’s military presence in border areas of northern Ethiopia and its cultivation of relationships with armed groups operating inside Ethiopian territory. For more than a year, Ethiopian authorities documented patterns of material support, including ammunition intercepts and alleged training linkages, directed toward elements of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front and other armed groups in Ethiopia. These activities culminated in formal Ethiopian notifications to the United Nations Security Council in October 2026, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter on the inherent right of self-defense in response to the advances of Eritrean units tens of kilometers into Tigrayan territory and coordination with domestic insurgent coalitions. The severing of diplomatic relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara in early October further removed remaining formal channels for crisis management. In this environment, Eritrea’s conduct has shifted from wartime alliance against the TPLF during 2020–2022 to a tactical realignment that treats a weakened or fragmented Ethiopian center as preferable to a consolidated neighbor capable of projecting power in the region. The nature of the regime, shaped by President Isaias Afwerki’s personalized style of rule and his longstanding political outlook towards Ethiopia, makes it unlikely that Asmara will voluntarily provide the guarantees necessary for de-escalation. For Ethiopia, however, Isaias’s decades-long rule has remained a persistent security concern, given Eritrea’s history of hostility towards its southern neighbor and its support for armed with anti-government agendas. Ethiopia needs credible guarantees from Eritrea to address these concerns, ease tensions, and create conditions for a lasting resolution. However, as noted above, the nature of Eritrea’s leadership makes such guarantees difficult to secure, particularly if they require a change in the security policies and political outlook that have shaped its approach towards Ethiopia for decades. Demands for an end to support for armed opposition groups, the cessation of cross-border arms transfers, and a verifiable halt to military preparations near Ethiopian territory would require the Eritrean leadership to reconsider practices closely tied to its system of internal control. Introduced during the 1998–2000 border war, national service has evolved into an indefinite obligation serving both military and labor needs. Many Eritreans remain in service for years, often with little control over their assignments and limited remuneration. Its prolonged nature also gives the government considerable influence over citizens’ livelihoods and their ability to leave state service. In Eritrea, generals often wield greater authority than civilian officials at the zonal level, with power ultimately concentrated in the presidency. Isaias Afwerki has also rotated military commanders and senior officials, limiting their ability to build independent power bases. Control over the economy, political coordination, information, and national security remains concentrated among a small circle of trusted figures whose influence depends heavily on their relationship with the president. Under such conditions, transparency and demobilization would be perceived as a threat to the regime’s capacity to extract resources, suppress dissent, and justify isolation. The empirical record of Eritrean foreign policy since its secession, marked by disputes with Yemen, Djibouti, Sudan, and Ethiopia, illustrates a consistent preference for confrontation over institutionalized cooperation when the latter would constrain personalist authority. In essence, full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would risk repeating the cost of the previous conflicts, while increasing the risk of regional actors becoming involved. A direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea would be an uneven contest given Ethiopia’s demographic and military scale. Yet Eritrea’s garrison-state structure would allow it to mobilize much of its population and national resources with potentially devastating consequences for its population and economy. Therefore, Ethiopia’s dilemma would be how to neutralize the threat posed by Eritrea’s leadership without turning the military imbalance into a prolonged and costly conflict. Given these constraints, effective threat neutralization begins with identifying the specific sources of risk. These include Eritrea’s military presence, support for armed groups, and other activities directed by its leadership that threaten Ethiopia’s security. Given the concentration of political and security authority within Eritrea’s leadership, a surgical and swift operation directed at the narrow decision-making and security core offers a theoretically coherent pathway. The personalist character of the Eritrean system concentrates operational and political authority in a limited set of individuals and institutions surrounding the president. However, this approach would require a carefully defined communication strategy to establish the basis for action, build international understanding of its security concerns and demonstrate that any measures taken are necessary and proportionate to the threats identified. Israel’s approach towards Iran illustrates how operations targeting senior leadership and key decision-making structures can disrupt command arrangements and weaken a state’s capacity to coordinate its response. However, Iran’s institutional depth has allowed it to sustain resistance despite the loss of senior figures. Eritrea differs in this respect, but the case provides an illustration. Its political system is more personalized, with authority concentrated around Isaias Afwerki and a narrow circle of military and security officials. Let alone the removal of the inner circle, the removal of Isaias would be consequential extending beyond Ethiopia’s immediate security concerns, potentially reshaping Eritrea’s political order and the wider Horn of Africa. Eritrea’s relatively shallow administrative depth, compared with more layered systems that possess provincial redundancy or institutionalized revolutionary guards, may increase the disruptive potential of precise action against the center. For international actors, Eritrea’s status as a pariah state, its record of playing a spoiler role in the region, and its government’s persistent human rights violations would shape how they assess such a development. The prospect of a change in leadership could be viewed as an opportunity to address longstanding sources of regional instability and the country’s human rights crisis. In its 2015 report, the UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea found that “systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations have been and are being committed in Eritrea under the authority of the Government,” adding that some of these violations “may constitute crimes against humanity.” Beyond this, such an approach could help avert a devastating interstate war, free the Eritrean people from a tyrannical and deeply oppressive regime and minimize wider humanitarian consequences. The broader regional context reinforces the logic of limitation. A major war would intersect with ongoing conflicts in Sudan, competition over Red Sea access, and Nile water disputes, creating opportunities for external actors to deeply embed themselves in the region. Eritrea’s alignment with SAF’s al-Burhan and Egypt mean that uncontrolled escalation would quickly expand the geographic and political scope of the conflict. By contrast, a tightly constrained operation that demonstrably prioritizes the neutralization of leadership-directed threats minimizes the grounds for third-party intervention and preserves Ethiopia’s capacity to address internal security challenges. The small-state syndrome that shapes Eritrean behavior is characterized by acute sensitivity to Ethiopia’s growing regional role and influence, alongside a tendency to use asymmetric means to constrain Ethiopia’s position and establish strategic buffer zones along its borders including through support for the TPLF. As noted, Eritrea’s political and security system is built around military mobilization, secrecy, and the use of regional networks to advance its strategic interests. For Ethiopia to achieve lasting security, Eritrea would need to provide credible assurances against military build-up, arms trafficking, and support for proxy groups, including the TPLF and other armed movements, while preventing its territory from being used as a sanctuary for groups seeking to destabilize Ethiopia. However, the centralized and highly personalized nature of Isaias Afwerki’s rule raises serious doubts about whether such commitments would be honored without meaningful pressure. Ethiopia’s long-term security interests therefore depend on addressing these sources of interference while avoiding the heavy costs of a prolonged interstate war. A carefully considered approach, supported by verified intelligence and a coherent communication strategy, seeks to address immediate security threats while preserving the prospects for long-term regional stability. Ethiopia cannot afford to remain trapped in the same recurring cycle of confrontation with Eritrea, in which unresolved threats repeatedly generate new tensions and bring both countries closer to a devastating war. Opening the three-day capacity development workshop today, Ethiopia's Auditor General Meseret Damtie said strengthening African Supreme Audit Institutions (SAIs) is essential in order to promote accountable governance, sound public financial management and sustainable development across the continent. She highlighted the importance of collaboration in strengthening institutions and advancing sustainable development, reflecting the program's emphasis on partnerships and collective efforts to improve public-sector accountability across Africa. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), he said the TPLF violated the Pretoria Agreement signed in October 2022. The PM recalled that the key elements of the Pretoria Agreement included cessation of hostilities, restoration of all services, disarmament, return of displaced people, and recognition of the constitutional order. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The federal government had fulfilled everything that was possible and expected of it, he added. On the contrary, the TPLF had been purchasing and soliciting weapons as well as openly recruiting young people instead of implementing the agreement to disarm combatants. Above all, PM Abiy pointed out that after the agreement, the TPLF used displaced persons as hostages to prevent them from returning to their homes. Additionally, it engaged in destroying and closing down infrastructure--including airlines, banking, and telecommunications--that had been restored by the Federal Government to deliver services. Despite the group's misdeeds, the PM stated that the government had forewarned that war was not worthwhile and that peace was preferable. However, the TPLF disregarded the advice and collaborated with various forces, and violated the Pretoria Agreement by initiating an unnecessary war. Immense damage has been inflicted on the public as a result of the war instigated by the TPLF, he noted. War is bad and yields no benefit, the Premier further noted, adding that a war fought for the interests of foreign forces is even worse. The psychological damage is not to be taken lightly and damage has also been inflicted on development and the economy. PM Abiy stressed that young people carrying Kalashnikovs should therefore return to work and participate in the development and rehabilitation of Tigray. Noting that many young people were forcibly recruited, he advised those who have not yet returned to return to normal life. He stated that the leaders of the TPLF have been declaring war for 50 years without dying or being wounded themselves; instead they sent their children and families abroad and to Addis Ababa where they are engaged in business and construction. The Premier highlighted the shared legacy of courage, unity, and sacrifice between the two countries. In a social media post, the Prime Minister said: "I delivered remarks paying tribute to the heroes who fought for freedom and those who made the ultimate sacrifices to safeguard their nation. I honour their courage and legacy!" PM Abiy noted that Kenya's history of courage and sacrifice resonates deeply with Ethiopia's own story of Adwa, where Ethiopians from every corner of the country united to defend their homeland. These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given but won through courage, unity, and sacrifice, the Prime Minister added. "As our histories are intertwined, so too must our futures be. Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people," he said. The two countries also cooperate in regional security, cross-border infrastructure, trade, telecommunications, and electricity interconnections, supporting economic integration and development across the Horn of Africa, it was learned. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress
ethiopia.content: Africa: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress 21 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia has reformed its statistical legislation and established an independent statistical service to strengthen the production and coordination of official data, President Taye Atske Selassie said. Taye underscored the importance of reliable statistics in driving evidence-based development in Africa. Addressing the opening of the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the 12th Meeting of the Regional Committee of the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa in Addis Ababa, the President said Ethiopia's development planning is anchored in measurable targets and reliable data. He emphasized that development cannot be effectively planned, sustained, or scaled up without accurate measurement, noting that official statistics are essential for shaping development strategies, tracking progress, and strengthening accountability. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The President also highlighted Ethiopia's reforms in the financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy, financial sector liberalization, interoperable payment infrastructure, and the national digital identification program, Fayda. He said Fayda enables secure electronic verification and expands access to banking, mobile money, telecommunications, and other essential public services, demonstrating how digital infrastructure can improve service delivery and financial inclusion. According to the President, mobile money and mobile banking accounts in Ethiopia reached 257 million and processed more than 24 trillion birr in transactions during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting the expansion of the country's financial and digital systems. Drawing lessons from these reforms, he stressed that statistics must serve as practical tools for sustainable development and be communicated clearly and accessibly to policymakers and citizens, rather than being treated as an end in themselves. He also called for statistical institutions to integrate and safeguard diverse data sources without compromising statistical integrity, emphasizing that innovation must reinforce data quality, institutional independence, and public trust. The President urged African governments to protect the professional independence of official statistics, strengthen legal and institutional frameworks, invest in national statistical systems, and ground policy decisions in scientific evidence. He cautioned that poor-quality data undermines evidence-based policymaking, impedes development, and weakens accountability. The Premier highlighted the role of advanced technology in Ethiopia's long-term development ambitions. In a social media post following the visit, the Prime Minister said Ethiopia's next chapter of development would focus on translating its vast potential into tangible progress. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "Ethiopia's next chapter is about transforming its immense potential and abundant natural resources into tangible development, technological advancement, and shared prosperity," he underscored. He emphasized that reliable and sustainable energy is fundamental to industrialization, manufacturing, digital infrastructure, and broader economic transformation. He further noted that nuclear technology presents an opportunity to strengthen the country's energy security while supporting progress across multiple sectors. Beyond electricity generation, nuclear technology can contribute to advancements in healthcare, agriculture, industry, and environmental protection, opening new pathways for scientific innovation and sustainable development. The Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission plays a central role in establishing the institutional and technical foundations for the country's national nuclear energy program. Developing skilled human capital, advancing scientific research, and transferring knowledge to future generations will be critical to realizing its potential. Prime Minister Abiy underscored the importance of ensuring that nuclear energy development proceeds peacefully, safely, responsibly, and sustainably, as Ethiopia seeks to expand its energy capacity and harness emerging technologies to support its long-term economic transformation. somalia.content: Ethiopia, Kenya and the Growing Complexity of Somalia’s Security Crisis – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 Ethiopia, Kenya and the Growing Complexity of Somalia’s Security Crisis 0 Comments Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s visit to Kenya on October 20 came at a time when Ethiopia’s relations with its neighbours are increasingly shaped by competing security concerns and shifting regional alignments. Attending Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations as President William Ruto’s guest of honour, Abiy emphasized the longstanding partnership between the two countries, highlighting cooperation in electricity, telecommunications, trade and regional connectivity. Yet beyond the diplomatic celebrations, the visit coincided with growing tensions involving Somalia, whose internal political crisis has begun complicating its relations with both Ethiopia and Kenya. Although Abiy’s visit was officially centered on Kenya’s Mashujaa Day celebrations and bilateral cooperation, it unfolded against a backdrop of growing regional tensions involving Somalia. The visit did not publicly establish a common Ethiopian and Kenyan position on the Somali crisis, but it brought renewed attention to the strategic importance of their partnership as both countries navigate increasingly complicated relations with Mogadishu. The significance of Ethiopia’s relationship with Kenya extends beyond bilateral cooperation. Both countries have invested considerable military and diplomatic resources in Somalia’s stabilization, particularly in efforts to contain Al Shabaab and prevent insecurity from spreading across their borders. However, Somalia’s confrontation between its federal government and regional political actors is creating disagreements over the responsibilities of neighbouring countries. For Ethiopia, the challenge is to maintain its commitment to Somalia’s security without becoming involved in political disputes that could undermine its wider regional interests. The immediate source of tension lies in Somalia’s South West State, where the removal of former regional president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen in March 2026 failed to produce a lasting political settlement. Instead, confrontations between his supporters and forces aligned with the federal government have continued, exposing deeper disagreements over regional autonomy and the distribution of political authority. By October 19, forces loyal to Laftagareen reportedly controlled five towns in the Bay region, including Buurhakaba, Qansaxdheere and Dinsoor, complicating Mogadishu’s efforts to consolidate authority. The conflict is particularly consequential because the South West State includes territories where Ethiopian forces have maintained a security presence for years. According to Somali Guardian reporting published on October 19 , Somali federal authorities requested Ethiopian military assistance against forces aligned with Laftagareen, but Ethiopian commanders declined to participate in what they considered an internal political confrontation. Although the reported exchange has not been independently confirmed, it illustrates a fundamental question concerning foreign military involvement in Somalia: whether security assistance intended to confront common threats should extend to supporting the federal government in disputes over domestic political authority. For Ethiopia, the issue has acquired additional importance following the transition from the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, ATMIS, to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, AUSSOM, which commenced on January 1, 2025. Under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2767 , the successor mission was authorized to support Somali forces against Al Shabaab, protect civilians and facilitate the gradual transfer of security responsibilities to Somali institutions. Its mandate also encompasses security support for political processes, but does not provide unrestricted authority to determine the outcome of internal political disputes. The transition brought renewed attention to the distinction between Ethiopian troops operating under African Union arrangements and those deployed through separate bilateral security understandings. This distinction matters because forces assigned to AUSSOM operate within a defined multinational framework, while deployments outside that structure depend on separate arrangements with Somalia. In its December 2025 communiqué , the African Union Peace and Security Council explicitly acknowledged Ethiopia and Uganda for deploying additional troops under bilateral arrangements. Their presence cannot therefore be understood solely through AUSSOM’s command structure. Ethiopia’s longstanding involvement in Somalia has primarily been driven by the need to prevent Al Shabaab from developing secure operating areas near Ethiopian territory. The group’s ability to exploit instability and threaten communities across borders makes developments in Somalia directly relevant to Ethiopia’s national security. Ethiopian military operations and participation in successive African Union missions have consequently contributed to a broader effort to contain threats before they reach Ethiopian territory. The South West State remains especially important because the Bay and Bakool regions form part of the wider security environment connected to Ethiopia’s eastern frontier. Participation in Somalia’s internal political confrontations, however, would expose Ethiopia to different risks. Military intervention could associate Ethiopian forces with one Somali political faction, weaken relationships with local communities and transform a defined security commitment into an extended responsibility for political outcomes. Even a successful intervention would not necessarily resolve disagreements concerning federal authority and regional political representation. Somalia’s domestic disputes require political settlements that military involvement by neighbouring countries cannot independently deliver. This position should not be confused with opposition to Somalia’s federal government. Addis Ababa and Mogadishu continue to maintain diplomatic relations and share an interest in preventing renewed militant expansion. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s September 29 visit to Addis Ababa , during which he discussed bilateral relations and regional security with Abiy Ahmed, demonstrated the continued importance of diplomatic engagement despite existing disagreements. Those disagreements nevertheless have a deeper history. The January 2024 memorandum of understanding between Ethiopia and Somaliland, which addressed potential Ethiopian maritime access, produced a significant confrontation with Mogadishu over sovereignty and territorial integrity. Somalia regarded the arrangement as an infringement on its sovereignty, while Ethiopia viewed access to the sea as an important strategic and economic objective. The dispute contributed to Somalia’s closer security engagement with Egypt, which already maintained long winded Nile disagreements with Ethiopia. The December 2024 Ankara Declaration , facilitated by Türkiye, helped restore diplomatic engagement by reaffirming mutual respect for sovereignty and acknowledging the possibility of mutually beneficial maritime arrangements under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Nevertheless, restoring diplomatic communication did not eliminate competing regional security calculations. Egypt’s expanding security engagement with Somalia and its prospective contribution to AUSSOM have introduced further sensitivity into discussions about troop deployments. The African Union’s June 2025 negotiations with troop-contributing countries included Ethiopia and Egypt, demonstrating that both countries were considered within the mission’s institutional arrangements. In December 2025, the African Union also acknowledged Egypt’s preparations for deployment while emphasizing the need to prevent security gaps during the transition. Political endorsement, negotiated contributions and actual troop deployments, however, remain distinct stages. For Ethiopia, any substantial expansion of Egyptian forces near areas where Ethiopian troops operate would raise operational questions, particularly given the unresolved Nile dispute. Careful coordination would be essential to prevent competing strategic interests from complicating counterterrorism operations. Kenya faces a related challenge arising from Somalia’s domestic political confrontation. Laftagareen’s presence in Kenya following his removal has generated criticism from Somali officials. On October 19, Somalia’s parliamentary speaker, Abdikadir Mohamed Nur Jama, reportedly accused individuals residing in Kenya of involvement in activities connected to the conflict and questioned the alleged protection they received. The reporting did not establish evidence supporting those allegations, and Kenyan authorities had not publicly responded at the time. Hosting Somali political figures does not independently demonstrate Kenyan government support for their military activities. Nairobi must balance its diplomatic responsibilities and continued cooperation with Mogadishu against its own legal and national security considerations. The consequences of Somali instability for Kenya are also economic. The Lamu Port South Sudan Ethiopia Transport corridor, LAPSSET, represents an important regional infrastructure initiative intended to expand commercial connectivity and diversify access to maritime trade. Its security is connected to conditions in northern and coastal Kenya, where Al Shabaab has demonstrated the ability to threaten personnel and transport infrastructure. On September 19, 2026, suspected militants attacked Kenyan military personnel patrolling part of the corridor in Garissa. No casualties were reported, but the incident illustrated the security demands associated with protecting strategic infrastructure. Although these attacks cannot be directly attributed to the South West State’s political crisis, prolonged instability in Somalia could place additional pressure on counterterrorism operations and create opportunities for militant expansion. For Kenya, preserving security cooperation with Somalia therefore carries implications for domestic security, investment and regional transport connectivity. Ethiopia shares an interest in protecting these connections, which could strengthen economic integration and provide additional commercial routes. Against this background, the partnership between Addis Ababa and Nairobi offers continuity. Cooperation in electricity transmission, telecommunications and transport has created practical interests that extend beyond individual political disagreements. During his October 20 visit , Abiy emphasized Ethiopia’s electricity exports to Kenya, Safaricom’s presence in Ethiopia and growing commercial connections. Their importance becomes greater as Ethiopia confronts renewed tensions with Eritrea, instability in northern Ethiopia and unresolved strategic disagreements with Egypt. The October 2026 escalation in Tigray and tensions with Eritrea demonstrate the competing pressures confronting Addis Ababa. Strong relations with Kenya provide an additional channel for diplomatic consultation without requiring both governments to adopt identical policies toward Somalia. The coming months will test whether the three countries can prevent Somalia’s internal confrontation from developing into a wider regional dispute. Particular attention should be given to the security situation around Baidoa, changes to Ethiopian and Egyptian troop arrangements, and Somalia’s political preparations ahead of the presidential election announced for May 15, 2027 . Diplomatic engagement through Kenya, IGAD or other regional mechanisms could become increasingly relevant if political divisions deepen. Whether mediation initiatives emerge, however, will depend on the willingness of the parties to pursue negotiation. Abiy’s Kenya visit ultimately illustrates the continuing value of dependable regional partnerships during a period of uncertainty. Ethiopia’s national interests require a stable Somalia, effective cooperation against Al Shabaab and security arrangements that do not unnecessarily entangle Ethiopian forces in domestic political rivalries. Its relationship with Kenya offers opportunities to advance those objectives while protecting economic integration and regional connectivity. The challenge for Addis Ababa is to preserve this partnership alongside constructive engagement with Mogadishu, ensuring that Somalia’s political disagreements do not become another source of confrontation across the Horn of Africa.
